subject: Agriculture
title: Feudalism and the Land
description: Learn Feudalism and the Land in one minute.

hook.text: In feudal Europe, peasants didn't own the land they farmed. They owed labor and crops to their lord.

buildup.text: Serfs worked the lord's fields several days a week, then tended their own strips in remaining time.

discovery.text: In exchange, the lord provided protection and justice. The manor was a self-contained economic unit.

twist.text: Serfs couldn't leave. They were bound to the land—and passed that obligation to their children.

climax.text: The Black Death killed a third of Europe. Surviving peasants suddenly had bargaining power, and serfdom weakened.

punchline.text: Plague freed more peasants than any revolution did.

quiz.question: What event weakened serfdom across Europe?
options: The Black Death, which created a labor shortage
The invention of the printing press

details.summary: Feudalism organized medieval European society around land ownership and agricultural labor. This topic covers the manor system, serfdom, and how the relationship between lords and peasants shaped farming practices for centuries.
details.whyItMatters: Feudalism's legacy of highly concentrated land ownership persists in many countries today. Understanding its origins reveals why land reform remains one of the most contentious issues in global agriculture.
takeaways: Feudal manors were self-sufficient agricultural units centered on a lord's estate
Serfs were bound to the land and owed labor and a share of their harvest to lords
The feudal system provided stability but trapped peasants in poverty for generations

faq.question: How did feudalism organize agricultural production?
faq.answer: Under feudalism, lords owned the land and granted plots to peasants in exchange for labor and a portion of the harvest. The manor was a self-contained agricultural unit with common fields, pastures, woodlands, and a village of bound workers.

faq.question: What was life like for serfs under the feudal system?
faq.answer: Serfs were legally bound to the land, required to work the lord's fields several days per week, surrender part of their harvest, and pay for using the lord's mill and oven. They could not leave without permission but received military protection.
